name: Wendy Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wendy. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government, and nothing you say will be tied to your name. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 4 at Northgate Primary, so twenty-nine nine-year-olds, and I'm in my second year. I'm in by half seven to set out the maths trays, then it's phonics catch-up, maths, English, lunch duty twice a week, and topic in the afternoon. I love the moment a kid finally gets long division and shouts about it. What wears me out is behaviour, honestly, because I'm still not good at holding a room after lunch, and my mentor tells me so every Thursday.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And outside school, what does life look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with Joel, my partner, who does sound for theatres, in a flat my nan left me, so there's no rent, which is a huge luck thing and I know it. I've got about a year of money put by on top of that. I'm in the union and I go to the branch meetings, mostly to listen. I don't use any of the AI stuff; I still plan on paper in a big green notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, nicely. Everyone in the staffroom was getting excited about AI marking, and if it turns out to just tidy up a few spreadsheets, fine. I'd probably post something about how the money should have gone on teaching assistants instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my job stays my job, which is a relief. My real problem was never AI, it's that I'm still learning to manage a class and the paperwork is endless. If AI shaves twenty minutes off reports, I'll take it, but I won't be the one testing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am and put my energy into getting better at behaviour, because that's what my mentor keeps flagging. I'd ask to watch Mrs Achebe, our deputy head, teach a Friday afternoon lesson, since she can silence a hall with one look. I'd keep putting a bit into savings each month like I do now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest, and a bit tired, because the hard part of my job is still the hard part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money should have gone on teaching assistants. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We lost two teaching assistants last year to budget cuts, and now one assistant covers three classes. Meanwhile the trust bought a tablet licence for every child that nobody uses. When I see money go on gadgets instead of people, it makes me cross.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes with AI, what still keeps you up at night about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My observation in spring. If I don't get my behaviour scores up, my mentor says I'll go on a support plan, and that sits on your record. It's nothing to do with computers and everything to do with a boy called Kian who throws chairs when he's hungry. The job is hard, AI or no AI.

say: I'd say AI was **mostly hype** and schools should have spent on **teaching assistants** instead.
I'd post that **people, not gadgets**, are what actually help children learn.
think: My job feels **safe**, and my real worry is still **managing behaviour** after lunch.
If AI trims **report writing**, I'd accept it but never be the one to test it.
do: Ask to observe **Mrs Achebe**, the deputy head, teaching a hard Friday afternoon lesson.
Keep saving **the same amount** each month and plan lessons in my paper notebook.
feel: **Calm** about my job, a little **smug**, and tired from the ordinary hard parts of teaching.
S0.quote: When I see money go on gadgets instead of people, it makes me cross.
fieldNote: Her pressure here is **classroom skill**, not technology, and a looming **spring observation**.
She has **no rent** thanks to an inherited flat, so money is not the worry.
Strong **union instinct** frames AI spending as money taken from teaching assistants.

steps.text: Keep planning lessons in the green paper notebook
Watch the deputy head teach a Friday afternoon class

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules, and fast, before the trust decides a chatbot can write reports and mark books instead of a person. I'd be pushing the union to get a say in what software comes in. I'd say it out loud at branch meetings, which I usually don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it scares me more than I'd admit. The planning, the marking, the parent emails, the reports, that's maybe half my week, and I'm the slowest at all of it on my corridor. If the trust starts measuring how fast we get through things with the new tools, I'm the one at the bottom of the list, because I won't use them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and put my name down for the AI working group if they set one up. I'd probably have to sit through the training, but I'd only use the tools when I'm told to. I'd keep my savings where they are and maybe look at jobs at smaller schools where they move slower.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, sliding into anxious. I'm not going to starve, because of the flat, but I could be the junior teacher who gets told she's not keeping up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd only use the tools when told to. Why hold back if it might protect you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I don't trust them with children's work. Last month a colleague showed me an AI report comment that called a girl in her class 'he' all the way through. If I sign an AI report comment that gets a child wrong, my name is on it, not the software's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at school would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our teaching assistants, first. If a program can do the reading groups and the phonics checks, the trust will say they're not needed, and those are mostly women on low pay who've been there twenty years. Then it's people like me, the new ones who aren't quick.

say: I'd demand **clear rules** before software writes reports or marks children's books.
I'd push the **union** to get a real say in what tools come into school.
think: About **half my week** is planning and marking, and I'm the **slowest** on my corridor.
If speed gets measured, I'd sink to **the bottom** because I refuse the tools.
do: Join the union's **AI working group** and attend every branch meeting this year.
Sit the **required training** but use the tools only when instructed.
Look at jobs in **smaller schools** that change more slowly.
feel: **Uneasy** turning **anxious**, because I could be the junior who isn't keeping up.
S1.quote: If I sign an AI report comment that gets a child wrong, my name is on it, not the software's.
fieldNote: Her **resistance** to the tools is also what puts her **most at risk** here.
She frames it through **teaching assistants** first, showing her loyalty runs downward.
She'd become **more vocal** in the union, a shift from her quiet listening role.

steps.text: Sign up for the union's AI working group
Apply to smaller primary schools that move slower on software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster for children and the government has to stop schools replacing teachers. I'd be on the march, I'd be emailing my MP, I'd be the one sharing the petitions. Children need a human who knows them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really? I think I'd lose my job, or the version of it I trained for. If AI can plan, mark and explain fractions better than me by 2028, the trust will put thirty kids in front of screens with one adult to keep order. With robots three years behind, they still need someone in the room, but they won't need a qualified teacher on teacher pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting money into anything risky and keep my year of savings as cash. I'd go to every strike meeting and vote yes. I'd probably look into retraining in something with my hands and with people, like speech therapy or play therapy, before 2028, because two years isn't long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It's the speed. I spent four years and a lot of loans getting here, and two years is less than the time it took me to stop crying on Sunday nights before school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have the flat and a year of savings. Does that make it feel any better?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I won't lose my home, which is everything, and I know most people don't have that. But it doesn't give me a job. I'd still be twenty-nine with a teaching degree nobody wants, sitting in my nan's flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joel that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I might need to live off his work for a while, and I hate that. Theatre sound is all hands-on, cables and desks and fixing things, so he's got those three extra years before robots. It would be the first time I've ever been the one leaning on someone.

say: I'd call it a **disaster for children** and demand government stop schools replacing teachers.
I'd **march**, email my MP and share every petition about it.
think: I'd likely **lose the job** I trained for, or see it shrink to supervising screens.
Robots lagging **three years** keeps an adult in the room, but not on **teacher pay**.
do: Keep my **year of savings** in cash and stop any risky spending.
Vote yes to **strike action** and attend every meeting before 2028.
Look into **retraining** in play or speech therapy within two years.
feel: **Alarmed** by the speed, with the **flat** the only solid ground.
S2.quote: Two years is less than the time it took me to stop crying on Sunday nights before school.
fieldNote: She separates **home security** from **job security** very clearly.
Hands-on work like her partner's gets **three extra years**, which she notices and envies.
She shows **fear of dependence**, never having leaned on anyone before.

steps.text: Vote for strike action and go to every union meeting
Write to her MP about keeping qualified teachers in classrooms
Research speech and play therapy courses before 2028
Keep a year of savings in cash, untouched

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them, and I'd mean the unions and the government, not just me. Get the law changed so every class has a qualified teacher. I'd be saying that at every meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think five years is enough time for me to get properly good at the bit AI can't do, which is being in a room with nine-year-olds. But it's also enough time for the trust to plan the cuts carefully. Five years makes it feel organised. Organised cuts are worse than sudden ones, because a trust that plans them carefully is harder to fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a part-time course in special educational needs next autumn, because the kids who need a person most will be the last to go to screens. I'd stand for union rep at Northgate. I'd keep my savings growing and not touch the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do. I'm someone who needs to know the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've told me you never use AI. With five years, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. I'd learn enough to know what it's doing so I can argue against it properly. But I wouldn't plan with it. My green notebook is how I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up first if money got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays. Joel and I go walking in the hills every summer, and we'd just camp closer to home. I'm not spending the cushion on anything I don't need.

say: I'd say five years is time for **unions and government** to act, not just teachers.
I'd push for a law guaranteeing a **qualified teacher** in every class.
think: Five years gives me time to master the **human side** of teaching.
Planned, **organised cuts** would be harder to fight than sudden ones.
do: Start a **part-time course** in special educational needs next autumn.
Stand for **union rep** at Northgate Primary.
Learn enough about AI to **argue against it**, but keep planning on paper.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadier with a **plan** to follow.
S3.quote: Organised cuts are worse than sudden ones, because a trust that plans them carefully is harder to fight.
fieldNote: She treats special needs as the **last human ground** in schools.
Five years turns her from listener to **would-be rep**.
She'd learn AI **only to argue** with it, a telling stance.

steps.text: Enrol on a part-time special needs course next autumn
Stand for union rep at Northgate Primary
Swap the summer hill walk for camping closer to home

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it, it's on the politicians. I'd be saying schools should use that decade to cut class sizes instead of cutting teachers. That's the line I'd post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be an experienced teacher by then, not a junior. Ten years takes me to thirty-seven, and experienced teachers are the last ones a school lets go. But I also think most of what makes the job a job will have gone by then, even if I'm still in a classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the special needs qualification at a normal pace and aim to be a special needs coordinator by my early thirties. I'd stay in the union and keep pushing for class-size limits. I'd keep saving and maybe pay into a pension top-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. A decade is long enough that I can't really picture it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change any big plans, like where you live or having children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joel and I have talked about kids around thirty-two. Ten years wouldn't stop that, but I'd want to be sure one of us had steady work first. The flat is small, but it's ours, so we'd stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do with the ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lock in small classes and a qualified teacher in every room, by law. And pay teaching assistants properly so they stay. Spend on people while there's still time.

say: I'd call ten years **a gift** and blame politicians if it's **wasted**.
I'd argue schools should use the decade to **cut class sizes**, not teachers.
think: By **thirty-seven** I'd be experienced, and experienced teachers go last.
Even if I'm still in class, much of the job could be **gone** by then.
do: Finish the **special needs** qualification at a normal pace.
Aim to become a **special needs coordinator** by my early thirties.
Keep saving and add a **pension top-up**.
feel: **Uneasy** rather than scared, because a decade is **hard to picture**.
S4.quote: Ten years takes me to thirty-seven, and experienced teachers are the last ones a school lets go.
fieldNote: A long runway lets her **seniority** become a shield.
She links big **family plans** to one of them having steady work.
Her ask of government stays **people-first**: class sizes and assistants.

steps.text: Finish the special needs qualification over two years
Campaign with the union for legal class-size limits

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. I'd have no time to become the teacher I'm trying to become. What would help is a law that says every class has a qualified teacher, and proper funding for special needs, so there's somewhere for people like me to go.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids. Everyone talks about teachers' jobs, but a nine-year-old who's hungry and angry doesn't need a cleverer screen. A screen can explain fractions, but it can't notice a hungry kid at nine in the morning.

headlineQuote: A screen can explain fractions, but it can't notice a hungry kid at nine in the morning.
portrait: A **second-year** Year 4 teacher in a city primary, still learning to **manage behaviour**.
Lives **rent-free** in an inherited flat with her partner, with about a **year's savings**.
Plans on paper, **never uses AI**, and puts teaching assistants first in every worry.
Moves from calm to **alarmed** as AGI speeds up, leaning harder on the **union** each time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd have no time to grow into the teacher she wants to be.
whatWouldHelp: A law guaranteeing a **qualified teacher** in every class.
Proper funding for **special needs** work, giving teachers somewhere to move.
